claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: More than 50% of the animals feeding on E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine died within 24 hr.
claims.source: More than 50% of the animals feeding on E. coli lawns containing 1-hydroxyphenazine died within 24 hr, while animals feeding on control E. coli lawns or E. coli lawns containing other phenazines remained alive at the same time point (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: However, P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1G), suggesting that the addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
claims.source: However, P. aeruginosa mutants deficient in phenazine production were not compromised in their ability to kill C. elegans compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1G), suggesting that the addition of 1-hydroxyphenazine may have non-physiological effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phenazine mutants are not attenuated in killing, yet exogenous 1-hydroxyphenazine is highly toxic.

claims.claim: All the phenazine mutants induced an avoidance behavior that was indistinguishable from that caused by the wild-type P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: Moreover, all the phenazine mutants induced an avoidance behavior that was indistinguishable from that caused by the wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The normal amount of phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa during infection is insufficient for induction of the avoidance behavior.
claims.source: These results suggest that while high amounts of externally added 1-hydroxyphenazine elicit microbial avoidance behavior, the normal amount of phenazines produced by P. aeruginosa during infection is insufficient for induction of the avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that phenazine mutants still induce avoidance.

claims.claim: The initial phase of interaction before elicitation of the avoidance behavior is variable, leading to different avoidance kinetics in various studies.
claims.source: However, the initial phase of interaction before elicitation of the avoidance behavior is variable, leading to different avoidance kinetics in various studies (Hao et al., 2018; Hilbert and Kim, 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017; Meisel et al., 2014; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Sun et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies showing variability.

claims.claim: Variations in avoidance kinetics are likely due to differences in the production of P. aeruginosa factors governing the avoidance behavior.
claims.source: It is likely that the variations in avoidance kinetics are due to differences in the production of P. aeruginosa factors governing the avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain observed variability.

claims.claim: Different growing conditions for the P. aeruginosa lawns might be responsible for the differences in avoidance behaviors.
claims.source: We reasoned that different growing conditions for the P. aeruginosa lawns might be responsible for the differences in avoidance behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: One of the major differences in bacterial lawn preparations is the variation in incubation periods of P. aeruginosa on agar plates before animal exposure.
claims.source: We observed that one of the major differences in bacterial lawn preparations is the variation in incubation periods of P. aeruginosa on agar plates before animal exposure (Hao et al., 2018; Hilbert and Kim, 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Meisel et al., 2014; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Sun et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of methods in cited studies.

claims.claim: The avoidance behavior of the animals was enhanced with the incubation period of the P. aeruginosa lawns.
claims.source: The avoidance behavior of the animals was enhanced with the incubation period of the P. aeruginosa lawns (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns incubated at 37°C for 24 hr followed by 25°C for 48 hr showed a significantly enhanced avoidance rate compared to animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns incubated at 37°C for 12 hr.
claims.source: Animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns that were incubated at 37°C for 24 hr followed by 25°C for 48 hr (referred to as 72 hr lawn) showed a significantly enhanced avoidance rate in comparison to animals exposed to P. aeruginosa lawns that were incubated at 37°C for 12 hr (referred to as 12 hr lawn) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns.
claims.source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2D,E), animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns.
claims.source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed robust induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons that did not differ from animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2D,E), animals exposed to 12 hr lawns exhibited a delayed avoidance compared with animals exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons was not significantly different in animals exposed to 12 or 72 hr lawns.
claims.source: In addition, the induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons was not significantly different in animals exposed to 12 or 72 hr lawns (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ may not be the only cause of the elicitation of avoidance behavior.
claims.source: Because the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons was indistinguishable in animals on 12 and 72 hr lawns, the results suggest that the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ may not be the only cause of the elicitation of avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that daf-7 induction is similar but avoidance kinetics differ.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr.
claims.source: We found that animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr, while the lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claims.claim: The lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli.
claims.source: We found that animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed bloated intestines as early as 8 hr, while the lumens of animals exposed to 12 hr lawns for 8 hr were comparable to those of animals fed E. coli (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claims.claim: Bloating of the intestine leads to the induction of genes that are part of the NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathway.
claims.source: Because bloating of the intestine leads to the induction of genes that are part of the NPR-1 neuroendocrine pathway (Singh and Aballay, 2019a), we examined the expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3D, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns, but not to 12 hr lawns, showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns did not show higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3D, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns, but not to 12 hr lawns, showed higher expression levels of the npr-1, flp-18, and flp-21 genes compared with the control animals on E. coli.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of nol-6 reduces bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by bacterial infection.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated knockdown of nol-6, a nucleolar RNA-associated protein, reduces bloating of the intestinal lumen caused by bacterial infection (Fuhrman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi delayed pathogen avoidance.
claims.source: We found that nol-6 RNAi delayed pathogen avoidance (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Animals deficient in nol-6 failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr.
claims.source: Animals deficient in nol-6, which failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr (Figure 3E), did not exhibit intestinal bloating at the same time point when exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E-G.

claims.claim: Animals deficient in nol-6 did not exhibit intestinal bloating at 8 hr when exposed to 72 hr lawns.
claims.source: Animals deficient in nol-6, which failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr (Figure 3E), did not exhibit intestinal bloating at the same time point when exposed to 72 hr lawns (Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr.
claims.source: Consistent with the idea that bloating induces pathogen avoidance, nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr (Figure 3E), at which time they also exhibited intestinal bloating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi animals exhibited intestinal bloating at 24 hr when exposed to 72 hr lawns.
claims.source: Consistent with the idea that bloating induces pathogen avoidance, nol-6 RNAi animals exposed to 72 hr lawns avoided P. aeruginosa at 24 hr (Figure 3E), at which time they also exhibited intestinal bloating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior.
claims.source: These results indicate that nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior, and the delayed avoidance behavior is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nol-6 RNAi animals eventually avoid P. aeruginosa when bloating occurs.

claims.claim: The delayed avoidance behavior in nol-6 RNAi animals is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
claims.source: These results indicate that nol-6 RNAi animals are not generally defective in avoidance behavior, and the delayed avoidance behavior is due to delayed intestinal bloating.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between delayed bloating and delayed avoidance in nol-6 RNAi animals.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in ASJ neurons.
claims.source: Despite diminishing the avoidance behavior, knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in either ASJ (Figure 3H) or ASI neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons.
claims.source: Despite diminishing the avoidance behavior, knockdown of nol-6 did not affect the induction of daf-7 expression in either ASJ (Figure 3H) or ASI neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Bloating of the intestine, but not induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, underlies the avoidance behavior.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that bloating of the intestine, but not induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, underlies the avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that bloating correlates with avoidance while daf-7 induction does not.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization.
claims.source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure.
claims.source: We found that while animals exposed to 12 hr lawns showed a consistent increase in intestinal colonization, animals exposed to 72 hr lawns did not show any increase in colonization during the first 8 hr of exposure (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Intestinal bloating on 72 hr lawns is independent of bacterial colonization.
claims.source: These results indicate that intestinal bloating on 72 hr lawns is independent of bacterial colonization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that bloating occurs without increased colonization on 72 hr lawns.

claims.claim: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns.
claims.source: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns (Figure 4B), indicating that the virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
claims.source: Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns died significantly faster than animals exposed to 12 hr lawns (Figure 4B), indicating that the virulence of P. aeruginosa was higher on 72 hr than on 12 hr lawns.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the survival data showing faster death on 72 hr lawns.

claims.claim: A non-virulent P. aeruginosa strain deficient in the gene gacA fails to elicit C. elegans avoidance.
claims.source: It has been shown that a non-virulent P. aeruginosa strain deficient in the gene gacA, a global activator of gene expression and virulence, fails to elicit C. elegans avoidance (Hao et al., 2018; Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa gacA mutants are hampered in the induction of daf-7 in the ASJ chemosensory neuron.
claims.source: P. aeruginosa gacA mutants are also hampered in the induction of daf-7 in the ASJ chemosensory neuron (Meisel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: All studied P. aeruginosa mutants exhibited reduced virulence compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: We confirmed that all the studied P. aeruginosa mutants exhibited reduced virulence compared with wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: All studied P. aeruginosa mutants were deficient in the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior.
claims.source: All of these mutants were also deficient in the elicitation of pathogen avoidance behavior (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons.
claims.source: We found that while kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, the induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: The induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: We found that while kinB and rhlR mutants of P. aeruginosa were deficient in the induction of daf-7 in ASJ neurons, the induction of daf-7 by lasR, lysC, and ptsP mutants was comparable to the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claims.claim: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons by all studied P. aeruginosa mutants was indistinguishable from the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: The induction of daf-7 expression in ASI neurons by all of these P. aeruginosa mutants was indistinguishable from the induction by wild-type P. aeruginosa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The levels of daf-7 induction in the ASJ neurons induced by different P. aeruginosa mutants did not show any correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns.
claims.source: The levels of daf-7 induction in the ASJ neurons induced by different P. aeruginosa mutants did not show any correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The mean survival of the animals on different P. aeruginosa mutants showed a strong correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns.
claims.source: In contrast, the mean survival of the animals on different P. aeruginosa mutants showed a strong correlation with the mean occupancy of the animals on P. aeruginosa mutant lawns (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The virulence of P. aeruginosa, and not its ability to induce daf-7 in ASJ neurons, correlates with C. elegans avoidance behavior.
claims.source: Taken together, these results show that the virulence of P. aeruginosa, and not its ability to induce daf-7 in ASJ neurons, correlates with C. elegans avoidance behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing correlation between virulence and avoidance but not between daf-7 induction and avoidance.

claims.claim: Prior exposure to P. aeruginosa for several hours enables C. elegans to preferentially choose nonpathogenic E. coli over P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: It is known that prior exposure to P. aeruginosa for several hours enables C. elegans to preferentially choose nonpathogenic E. coli over P. aeruginosa (Zhang et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: When naïve animals were given a choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa, the animals changed their preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli after 8 hr of exposure.
claims.source: Similarly, in a two-choice assay, when naïve animals were given a choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa, the animals changed their preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli after 8 hr of exposure (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Aerotaxis plays a role in pathogen avoidance.
claims.source: Because aerotaxis plays a role in pathogen avoidance (Meisel et al., 2014; Reddy et al., 2009; Singh and Aballay, 2019a; Styer et al., 2008), we examined whether aerotaxis is also important for changes in preference from pathogenic to nonpathogenic bacteria.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa lawns have lower oxygen levels than E. coli lawns.
claims.source: It is known that P. aeruginosa lawns have lower oxygen levels than E. coli lawns (Gray et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Expression of the gene cysl-2 is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1).
claims.source: Expression of the gene cysl-2 is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), a transcription factor that is induced by low levels of oxygen (Ma et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels.
claims.source: Since HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels (Jiang et al., 2001), the expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
claims.source: Since HIF-1 is degraded at higher and accumulates at lower oxygen levels (Jiang et al., 2001), the expression levels of cysl-2 correlate inversely with the oxygen levels experienced by the animals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known regulation of HIF-1 by oxygen levels.

claims.claim: Animals exposed for 24 hr to P. aeruginosa lawns had higher GFP levels compared with those exposed to E. coli lawns.
claims.source: We found that animals exposed for 24 hr to P. aeruginosa lawns had higher GFP levels compared with those exposed to E. coli lawns (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: Loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1 inhibited pathogen avoidance.
claims.source: We observed that the loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1, which are deficient in DAF-7/TGF-β, and NPR-1 signaling, respectively, inhibited both pathogen avoidance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1 inhibited the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli.
claims.source: We observed that the loss of function mutants daf-7 and npr-1, which are deficient in DAF-7/TGF-β, and NPR-1 signaling, respectively, inhibited both pathogen avoidance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) and the change in preference from P. aeruginosa to E. coli (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1 signaling pathways act in parallel.
claims.source: These two neuroendocrine pathways are known to act in parallel (Chang et al., 2006; de Bono et al., 2002); therefore, we investigated the behaviors of daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The phenotypes of pathogen avoidance and change in preference were enhanced in daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals.
claims.source: We found that the aforementioned phenotypes were enhanced in daf-7(ok3125);npr-1(ad609) animals (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Aerotaxis-regulating pathways are required for the change in microbial preference upon pathogen infection.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that aerotaxis-regulating pathways are required for the change in microbial preference upon pathogen infection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that mutations in aerotaxis pathways prevent preference changes.

claims.claim: The increased preference for low oxygen in loss of function npr-1 and daf-7 mutants requires the function of the TRPV genes osm-9 and ocr-2.
claims.source: The increased preference for low oxygen in loss of function npr-1 and daf-7 mutants requires the function of the transient receptor potential channel vanilloid (TRPV) genes osm-9 and ocr-2 (Chang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Loss of function ocr-2 and osm-9 mutants have an increased preference for high oxygen levels.
claims.source: Because loss of function ocr-2 and osm-9 mutants have an increased preference for high oxygen levels (Chang et al., 2006), and because E. coli lawns have relatively higher oxygen levels (Gray et al., 2004; Reddy et al., 2011), we reasoned that these mutants should rapidly change their preference to E. coli if given the choice between E. coli and P. aeruginosa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals exhibited a strong enhancement of avoidance behavior.
claims.source: As expected, ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals exhibited a strong enhancement of avoidance behavior (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) animals showed a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
claims.source: These animals also showed a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The preference for high oxygen in ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) mutants is suppressed by the loss of function mutation in egl-9.
claims.source: The preference for high oxygen in ocr-2(ak47) and osm-9(yz6) mutants is suppressed by the loss of function mutation in egl-9, a negative regulator of HIF-1 (Chang and Bargmann, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The egl-9 mutation suppressed both the enhanced pathogen avoidance and E. coli preference of osm-9(yz6) animals.
claims.source: Consistent with the function of EGL-9, we observed that the egl-9 mutation suppressed both the enhanced pathogen avoidance and E. coli preference of osm-9(yz6) animals (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: Aerotaxis regulates both P. aeruginosa avoidance and changes in microbial preference.
claims.source: These results show that aerotaxis regulates both P. aeruginosa avoidance and changes in microbial preference.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that genetic manipulation of aerotaxis affects both avoidance and preference.

claims.claim: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways.
claims.source: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways, which results in a preference towards high oxygen (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection results in a preference towards high oxygen.
claims.source: Bloating of the intestinal lumen upon pathogen infection activates the NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β pathways, which results in a preference towards high oxygen (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aex-5 and egl-8 caused bloating of the intestinal lumen and led to enhanced avoidance of P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: Knockdown of these genes caused bloating of the intestinal lumen and led to enhanced avoidance of P. aeruginosa (Singh and Aballay, 2019a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Inhibition of aex-5 and egl-8 by RNAi and mutations elicited a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6E,F, inhibition of these genes by RNAi and mutations also elicited a rapid change in preference to E. coli lawns in the two-choice assay.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claims.claim: Exposure to 5% oxygen elicited a rapid preference towards E. coli.
claims.source: We were also able to elicit a rapid preference towards E. coli by exposing the animals to 5% oxygen (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Exposure to low oxygen levels alone does not affect either intestinal bacterial colonization or bloating.
claims.source: Exposure to low oxygen levels alone does not affect either intestinal bacterial colonization or bloating (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi animals are resistant to P. aeruginosa infection and bloating.
claims.source: We studied the change in microbial preference in nol-6 RNAi animals that are resistant to P. aeruginosa infection and bloating.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior characterization of nol-6 RNAi animals and data shown earlier in the manuscript.

claims.claim: nol-6 RNAi animals were defective in aversive learning toward P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6G, nol-6 RNAi animals were defective in aversive learning toward P. aeruginosa.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Intestinal bloating caused by pathogen infection is important for the learning process that leads to change in microbial preference from bacterial lawns containing relatively lower to those containing relatively higher oxygen levels.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that intestinal bloating caused by pathogen infection, which modulates aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways, is important for the learning process that leads to change in microbial preference from bacterial lawns containing relatively lower to those containing relatively higher oxygen levels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the neuroendocrine pathways NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β that control aerotaxis behavior.
claims.source: Our study establishes that intestinal infection and bloating of the lumen, which depend on the virulence of P. aeruginosa, regulate both pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating the neuroendocrine pathways NPR-1/GPCR and DAF-7/TGF-β that control aerotaxis behavior (Figure 7).

results.result: Chemosensation of phenazines is insufficient for pathogen avoidance. Animals exposed to E. coli lawns containing phenazine-1-carboxamide, phenazine-1-carboxylic acid, or pyocyanin did not exhibit avoidance behavior, and phenazine mutants of P. aeruginosa induced avoidance indistinguishable from wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C31, C32, C41, and C42 collectively demonstrate through multiple lines of evidence (Figures 1B, 1H) that phenazines alone do not elicit avoidance. The data show that exogenous phenazines (except 1-hydroxyphenazine) fail to induce avoidance, and phenazine-deficient mutants retain full avoidance capacity, strongly supporting the conclusion that chemosensation of phenazines is insufficient for this behavior.

results.result: 1-hydroxyphenazine causes intestinal bloating and avoidance but has non-physiological effects. While exogenous 1-hydroxyphenazine induced both bloating and avoidance, phenazine-deficient P. aeruginosa mutants were not attenuated in killing, suggesting the exogenous toxin effect does not reflect normal infection conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are well-supported by data in Figures 1C-G showing that 1-hydroxyphenazine causes bloating, avoidance, and lethality. However, the observation that phenazine mutants retain virulence (C39) appropriately leads to the inference that exogenous 1-hydroxyphenazine has non-physiological effects (C40), demonstrating critical interpretation of the results.

results.result: Avoidance kinetics depend on P. aeruginosa lawn incubation time, but daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons does not correlate with avoidance timing. Animals exposed to 72 hr lawns showed enhanced avoidance compared to 12 hr lawns, yet daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons was similar between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are strongly supported by data in Figures 2B-E showing differential avoidance kinetics despite equivalent daf-7 induction. This temporal mismatch between daf-7 activation (similar at both timepoints) and avoidance behavior (different kinetics) provides compelling evidence that daf-7 induction alone is insufficient to explain avoidance, supporting the manuscript's central thesis.

results.result: Intestinal bloating, not daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons, underlies avoidance behavior. Animals on 72 hr lawns showed bloating and elevated NPR-1 pathway gene expression at 8 hr, while 12 hr lawn animals did not, correlating with differential avoidance despite similar daf-7 induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, C56, C57, and C68 are well-supported by data in Figures 3A-D demonstrating correlation between bloating and avoidance. The observation that bloating differs between conditions while daf-7 induction does not provides strong evidence for the conclusion (C68) that bloating, rather than daf-7 induction, drives avoidance.

results.result: nol-6 knockdown delays pathogen avoidance by delaying intestinal bloating without affecting daf-7 induction. nol-6 RNAi animals failed to avoid P. aeruginosa at 8 hr when bloating was absent, but avoided at 24 hr when bloating occurred, while daf-7 induction remained unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C67 are strongly supported by data in Figures 3E-H and supplements showing temporal correlation between bloating and avoidance in nol-6 RNAi animals. The observation that daf-7 induction is unaffected (C66, C67) while avoidance is delayed provides additional evidence that bloating, not daf-7 induction, drives avoidance behavior.

results.result: Intestinal bloating on 72 hr lawns is independent of bacterial colonization and correlates with increased virulence. Animals on 72 hr lawns showed no increased colonization at 8 hr despite bloating, but died faster than animals on 12 hr lawns.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by data in Figures 4A-B showing differential colonization and survival patterns. The observation that bloating occurs without increased colonization (C71) is a valid inference from the data, though the mechanism remains unclear. The correlation between faster death and 72 hr lawns supports increased virulence (C73).

results.result: P. aeruginosa virulence, not daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons, correlates with avoidance behavior. Multiple attenuated P. aeruginosa mutants showed reduced avoidance despite variable daf-7 induction in ASJ neurons, with survival time showing strong correlation with avoidance (R²=0.97) while daf-7 levels did not (R²=0.038).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are strongly supported by comprehensive data in Figure 4 showing that virulence correlates with avoidance while daf-7 induction does not. The correlation analysis (C81, C82) provides quantitative support, and the diversity of mutants tested strengthens the conclusion (C83) that virulence, not chemosensation-induced daf-7, drives avoidance.

results.result: Aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways are required for learned preference changes from P. aeruginosa to E. coli. Animals changed preference after 8 hr exposure, P. aeruginosa lawns induced higher hypoxia marker expression, and daf-7 and npr-1 mutants showed impaired preference changes with enhanced defects in double mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C85, C91-C93, C95-C96 are well-supported by data in Figures 5A-G showing temporal preference changes, differential oxygen sensing, and genetic requirements. The synergistic effect in double mutants (C95) supports the conclusion that parallel aerotaxis pathways regulate preference changes (C96), though the precise mechanism linking infection to pathway modulation requires further investigation.

results.result: Genetic manipulation of aerotaxis drives rapid preference changes and enhanced avoidance. ocr-2 and osm-9 mutants with increased high-oxygen preference showed enhanced avoidance and rapid E. coli preference, with egl-9 mutations suppressing these phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C100, C102, and C103 are strongly supported by data in Figure 6A-D demonstrating that genetic modulation of aerotaxis is sufficient to alter both avoidance and preference behaviors. The epistasis analysis with egl-9 (C102) provides mechanistic insight linking oxygen sensing to behavioral outputs, supporting the conclusion (C103).

results.result: Intestinal bloating modulates aerotaxis pathways to drive learned preference changes. Genetic induction of bloating (aex-5, egl-8 mutants) and hypoxia exposure elicited rapid E. coli preference, while bloating-resistant nol-6 RNAi animals were defective in aversive learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C107, C108, C111, and C112 are well-supported by data in Figures 6E-G showing that bloating is both necessary (nol-6 RNAi) and sufficient (aex-5/egl-8 mutants, hypoxia) for preference changes. The convergence of genetic and environmental manipulations strongly supports the conclusion (C112) that bloating-mediated aerotaxis modulation drives learning.

results.result: Intestinal infection and bloating regulate pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating NPR-1 and DAF-7 pathways that control aerotaxis. Enhanced pathway activity leads to low-oxygen avoidance, driving movement from P. aeruginosa to E. coli lawns and enabling learned preference changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 represent the manuscript's central conclusions, synthesizing results from all experiments. These claims are well-supported by the cumulative evidence showing: (1) bloating correlates with avoidance, (2) virulence determines bloating, (3) aerotaxis pathways are required, and (4) genetic/environmental manipulation of these pathways is sufficient. The model is illustrated in Figure 7 and represents a coherent integration of the data.

results.result: DAF-7/TGF-β pathway activity is required but its rapid chemosensory activation is insufficient for avoidance; animals likely integrate multiple inputs including bloating and chemosensation. The pathways are induced by bloating and act synergistically to elicit avoidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C126 are supported by data showing daf-7 mutants lack avoidance (Figure 5—supplement 1A) while rapid daf-7 induction doesn't correlate with avoidance timing. The synergistic action of DAF-7 and NPR-1 pathways (C125, Figure 5G) and their induction by bloating (C124, cited prior work) support the integration model (C126), though direct mechanistic evidence for integration is limited.

results.result: Bloating-mediated modulation of aerotaxis pathways is required for aversive learning, and genetic modulation of aerotaxis can induce rapid preference changes. The learning process involves intestinal bloating modulating aerotaxis-regulating neuroendocrine pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are well-supported by data in Figures 5-6 showing that bloating is required (nol-6 RNAi defect) and that genetic aerotaxis modulation is sufficient (ocr-2/osm-9 mutants) for preference changes. The mechanistic link between bloating and pathway modulation is supported by gene expression data (Figure 3D) and prior work, though direct pathway activity measurements during learning would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Exposure to low oxygen levels alone does not affect intestinal bacterial colonization or bloating.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is supported by data in Figure 6—supplement 3 showing that 8% oxygen exposure does not cause bloating or affect colonization. This control experiment is important for distinguishing direct oxygen effects from infection-mediated effects, supporting the interpretation that bloating during infection, not oxygen levels per se, drives behavioral changes.

results.result: P. aeruginosa phenazines, particularly phenazine-1-carboxamide, activate DAF-7/TGF-β expression in ASJ neurons within minutes of exposure, with no further changes up to 24 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C16, C30, C119, and C120 are supported by citations to prior work (Meisel et al., 2014) establishing the rapid chemosensory response. While this study does not independently verify these kinetics, the claims accurately represent established prior findings that form the basis for the current investigation into why this rapid response is insufficient for avoidance.

results.result: Intestinal infection and bloating, dependent on P. aeruginosa virulence, regulate pathogen avoidance and aversive learning by modulating DAF-7/TGF-β and NPR-1 pathways. This modulation serves as systemic feedback enabling avoidance and modulates behavior, learning, and microbial perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8, C22-C25, and C118 represent the manuscript's overarching conclusions. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence showing virulence-dependent bloating (Figure 4), pathway modulation (Figure 3D), genetic requirements (Figures 5-6), and sufficiency of pathway manipulation (Figure 6). The claims appropriately synthesize the data into a coherent model of gut-brain signaling during infection.

results.result: The bloating-induced defense response might be a generalized response to pathogen infection enabling discrimination between pathogenic and innocuous microbes, possibly through pathogen-induced disturbance of intestinal pH waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C135, C136, and C143 are speculative extrapolations beyond the data. While C135 and C136 are reasonable hypotheses supported by cited work showing multiple pathogens cause bloating, they remain untested in this study. C143 regarding pH wave disturbance is purely speculative. These represent interesting future directions but lack direct experimental support in the current manuscript.
